chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hanan ibn Sudeyr who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked — and I was present with him — about a kid (baby goat) that was breastfed by a female pig until it grew big, matured, and its bones became strong. Then a man used it as a stud among his flock, so offspring were produced from it.

So he (peace be upon him) said: As for what you recognize from its offspring specifically, do not go near it. As for what you do not recognize, then eat it — for it is at the status of cheese, and do not ask about it.

key_terms.اسْتَفْحَلَهُ: Used it as a stud/sire for breeding; key verb establishing the concern about transmitted impurity through lineage
key_terms.بِعَيْنِهِ: Specifically/exactly; distinguishes definite knowledge from uncertainty in applying the prohibition
key_terms.بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْجُبُنِّ: At the status/level of cheese; a legal analogy used by the Imam to establish that one does not inquire into uncertain origins when the item appears permissible
key_terms.جَدْي: Kid (baby goat); used here to introduce a jurisprudential question about an unusual case of cross-species nursing

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating offspring of a goat raised on pig's milk according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) was asked about the jurisprudential ruling on offspring produced by a male goat that was raised on pig's milk. The Imam established a principle of permissibility based on certainty: only animals definitively identified as descendants of the pig-milk-fed goat are forbidden; unidentifiable ones are presumed halal — analogous to the well-established ruling on cheese, where one does not inquire into the exact nature of the rennet used. This reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that uncertainty does not negate presumed permissibility (asalat al-ibaha).
